text: The default scheduler already picks a reasonable node for every Pod, but reasonable isn't always correct. Northbridge's GPU recommendation service needs GPU nodes specifically, and checkout replicas need to spread across nodes for resilience. Taints, tolerations, and affinity give direct control over placement.

nodeSelector is the simplest option — an exact label match, nothing more. Node affinity replaces it for anything more expressive, with a required strength that behaves like nodeSelector, and a preferred strength that's just a soft preference the scheduler tries but won't force.

Where affinity pulls Pods toward nodes, a taint repels them — a tainted node rejects any Pod without a matching toleration. NoSchedule blocks new Pods, PreferNoSchedule softly avoids it, and NoExecute even evicts Pods already running there that don't tolerate it.

Pod affinity and anti-affinity place a Pod relative to other Pods, not node labels. Anti-affinity on checkout's own label tells the scheduler not to put two checkout replicas on the same node — real protection against a single node failure taking the whole service down.

That closes out Chapter 5 — resource limits keep Pods from starving each other, health probes catch what's actually broken, the HPA and Cluster Autoscaler respond to demand automatically, and scheduling controls decide exactly where it all runs.
